name: Hana Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Hana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. First, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Hana, I'm 27, and I work on my Uncle Erik's farm at Lindholm, where my family has farmed for four generations. It's wheat and barley, about 3,000 laying hens for free-range eggs, and a small herd of beef cows. I'm paid like any worker, and a good wage, and Dad left me 30 acres that Uncle Erik farms alongside his own. I'm courting Mikkel, who works at the agricultural merchants in town, and we're at church together every Sunday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Eggs first, every day of the year: collecting, checking the hens, grading and packing for the shops in town. Then whatever Uncle Erik needs, feeding the cows, fixing a door, carting grain in harvest. I'm still learning the arable side, he won't let me near the combine yet, and he's probably right. I love the hens in the evening when they settle, and I love Sundays. What wears me out is the egg grading machine breaking and Uncle Erik swearing at it in two languages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. People always get excited about something new from the cities, and then the cows still need feeding. I'd say that after church, and Pastor Lund would agree with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be glad. I never wanted it, and I don't trust things I can't see working. If it all comes to nothing, the farm carries on and so do I.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, same as now. Ask Uncle Erik to teach me the combine this harvest. Keep saving, because Mikkel and I want to marry in a year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anyone in your family use these AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Lars, who's at the agricultural college. He's always on his phone asking it things. Uncle Erik calls it Lars's oracle and asks him to put it away at dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you want the farm to look like in ten years, if nothing big changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as it is, but with me doing more of it. Maybe Mikkel and me in the old cottage by the barn. Maybe children running about the yard, like I did.

S0.say: She'd say people always get excited about something new from the cities, and then the cows still need feeding. She'd say it after church.
S0.think: Privately she'd be glad, because she never wanted it and doesn't trust things she can't see working. The farm carries on and so does she.
S0.do: Keeps going as normal and asks her uncle to teach her the combine at harvest. Keeps saving towards marrying her partner in a year or two.
S0.quote: Uncle Erik calls it Lars's oracle and asks him to put it away at dinner.
S0.fieldNote: Hana's world is family, church and the farm, and she sees AI as something from outside it. Her money is secure because of family land and a good wage. Her picture of the future is one of continuity, with marriage and children on the same yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities will see us through, like they always have. I'd say people should work and learn a trade, not wait for the government. That's what my dad would have said.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me a little. Uncle Erik is family, but he's also a businessman, and Lars will come back from college full of ideas. I'm the one who does the eggs, and eggs is the part a machine could take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and work harder, so nobody could say I'm not worth it. I'd wait and see what Uncle Erik decides, and I wouldn't argue. I'd keep the money in the bank and not spend on anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A small stone in my boot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your uncle bring in machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was proven, yes. He's not against new things, just against paying for things that break. And Lars would push him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the eggs? Could a machine do your job there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Collecting, maybe, there are machines that do that on big farms already. But checking the hens, seeing which one's off colour or being pecked, that needs someone who knows them. At least I hope so.

S1.say: She'd say families and communities will see people through, like they always have. People should work and learn a trade, not wait for the government.
S1.think: Privately she's a little worried: her uncle is a businessman too, and her cousin will come home full of ideas. The eggs are her job and the part a machine could take.
S1.do: Keeps going and works harder to show her worth. Waits to see what her uncle decides and holds off on any new spending.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a small stone in her boot.
S1.quote: Uncle Erik is family, but he's also a businessman, and Lars will come back from college full of ideas.
S1.fieldNote: Her family ties protect her, but she's honest that they aren't a guarantee. She'd answer change by working harder rather than learning anything new. The cousin with his oracle is the quiet threat in her story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is wrong, and that something made by people in the cities is being pushed on everyone else. I'd pray about it, and I'd say so. I'm not one for marches, but I'd tell anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it frightens me. Not because we'd go hungry, we've got land. Because if a robot does the eggs and the cows and the harvest, then what is Lindholm for? What do I teach my children?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the land, whatever else happened, because land is land. Mikkel and I would marry sooner, this year, and settle on the farm properly. I'd lean on family and the church, and I'd hold on to every penny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be awake at night thinking about Dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You have land of your own. What does that mean here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means we eat, and it means I belong somewhere. Uncle Erik might sell up and buy robots, but my 30 acres stay mine. I'd grow what I could on them myself, even if it made no money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you turn for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, then the church. Pastor Lund would get people together, he always does when there's trouble. Not the government, unless there was no other way.

S2.say: She'd say this is wrong, and something made in the cities is being pushed on everyone. She'd pray about it and say so, but she's not one for marches.
S2.think: Privately it frightens her, not for money but for meaning. If robots do everything, she asks what the farm is for and what she would teach her children.
S2.do: Keeps working the land whatever happens and marries her partner this year to settle on the farm. Leans on family and church and holds on to every penny.
S2.feel: Alarmed, awake at night thinking about her late father.
S2.quote: If a robot does the eggs and the cows and the harvest, then what is Lindholm for? What do I teach my children?
S2.fieldNote: Her fear is about meaning and inheritance rather than income, which is striking given how secure her finances are. Marrying sooner is her response, not retraining. She'd turn to family and church before any government help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say young people should get trades and apprenticeships now, while there's time. Families should help their own. I'd say it at the church harvest supper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is still fast, but it's long enough to get the land in order. I won't change who I am in five years. But I can make sure the farm stays in the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd talk to Uncle Erik about putting my 30 acres into a proper family arrangement, so it can't be sold off. I'd look at buying the field next to mine if it came up. We'd marry next year as planned and keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But there's time to put things right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two years doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to get the paperwork and the land sorted, really. With two years I'd just hold on. With five I'd build something to hand down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about learning any new skills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the cattle side, so I'm more useful. But not computers. I know that's stubborn, Mikkel tells me so. I'd rather be good at what I know.

S3.say: She'd say young people should get trades and apprenticeships now, while there's time, and families should help their own.
S3.think: Privately she thinks five years is still fast but long enough to get the land in order. She won't change who she is, but she can keep the farm in the family.
S3.do: Talks to her uncle about a family arrangement so her 30 acres can't be sold, and looks at buying the neighbouring field. Marries next year as planned and keeps saving.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with time to put things right.
S3.quote: With two years I'd just hold on. With five I'd build something to hand down.
S3.fieldNote: Her plan with five years is about land and inheritance, not skills. She openly refuses to learn computers and calls herself stubborn. The extra time turns fear into a sense of duty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and we should use it the old way: work hard, look after family, keep the land. I'd say it to anyone who asked. I'd still not be on any internet forum about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years makes it feel further off than it probably is. I'd tell myself I've got time. I'd likely do nothing until the last few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, marry, buy more land if it comes up. I'd keep saving and wait to see what Uncle Erik and Lars do with the farm before I did anything myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's a cloud on the horizon, but far off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years from now you'd be 37. What would you want in place by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Children, I hope. The land in my name, the cottage, the hens. A family that knows how to farm, even if the robots do most of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time change how you feel about the machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. With ten years, maybe some machines are fine, as long as the family owns them. I wouldn't want to run them, but I'd let Lars.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is a long time and should be used the old way: work hard, look after family and keep the land.
S4.think: Privately she thinks ten years makes it feel further off than it is, and she'd tell herself she has time. She expects to do nothing until the last few years.
S4.do: Keeps going, marries and buys more land if it comes up. Keeps saving and waits to see what her uncle and cousin do with the farm before acting.
S4.feel: Uneasy, like a far-off cloud on the horizon.
S4.quote: A family that knows how to farm, even if the robots do most of it.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years she softens slightly on machines, as long as the family owns them and someone else runs them. She predicts her own delay with candour. Land and children stay at the centre of every plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it would take the farm's meaning before we could do anything. What would help is people sticking together, families and churches, and a rule that land can't just be bought up by robot companies.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about faith. Everyone asks about jobs and money. But on Sunday the whole valley is in one room, and no machine is going to take that.

headlineQuote: On Sunday the whole valley is in one room, and no machine is going to take that.
portrait: Hana Jensen is a 27-year-old junior worker on her uncle's family farm at Lindholm, with grain, laying hens and beef cows, and she owns 30 acres left to her by her father. She's traditional, rooted in her church and her family, and has never used AI. Her money is safe, but the fast AGI picture alarms her because it threatens what the farm means and what she'd pass on. With more time she focuses on keeping the land in the family, marrying and having children, while admitting she'd probably wait too long to act.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would take away the farm's meaning before the family could do anything.
whatWouldHelp: Families and churches sticking together, and a rule stopping robot companies from buying up land.
